# From Hamilton-Jacobi–Bellman to Riccati via Carleman: The Scalar Case

Philip J. Elias<sup>1</sup>, Qiyu Sun<sup>2</sup>, and Nader Motee<sup>3</sup>

**_Abstract_--The Hamilton-Jacobi–Bellman (HJB) equation of a nonlinear system is a nonlinear partial differential equation, and in that form it gives little away. This paper shows that it hides a Riccati equation. Carleman linearization reveals this structure. For scalar analytic input-affine systems, the lifted HJB equation is a single infinite-dimensional Riccati equation in a lower-triangular Toeplitz matrix. Its first entry is the Riccati equation of the standard linearization at equilibrium. Its remaining entries hold the nonlinear terms. Nothing about this is an approximation. Under controllability of the standard linearization and detectability of the cost, the equation has exactly one solution with positive diagonal entries, and it can be computed one entry at a time. This solution is the derivative of the value function. We prove that finite-sections of the solution are exact and converge exponentially to the derivative of the value function near the origin. The scalar case has a closed-form solution. This closed form is our benchmark: every result on the lifted equation is checked against it. Nothing in this structure depends on the state dimension. Our methodology points to a general theory of optimal control in which the HJB equation of analytic nonlinear systems becomes an infinite-dimensional Riccati equation.**

### I. INTRODUCTION

We revisit a 1961 work by Al’brekht [1] on the power series approach to optimal control. He considered an analytic control system with an analytic cost and showed how to compute the optimal feedback near an equilibrium one term at a time. The first step is the linear-quadratic problem, as the quadratic part of the value function solves a Riccati equation. Each further term is then obtained from a linear equation whose right-hand side depends only on the terms already known. In 1969, Lukes [2] proved that the series converges and that the feedback it defines is optimal and stabilizing near the equilibrium, as long as the linearized system is stabilizable and detectable. Over the years, this recursion has become the standard tool to compute optimal feedback for smooth nonlinear systems. It has also been turned into algorithms and software [3]. In this paper, we turn the question around. Rather than computing the terms of the series individually, we ask what equation they satisfy together. Carleman linearization gives the answer. After lifting, all the terms of the series together solve a single infinite-dimensional Riccati-type equation, whose unknown is<tbc>

<tbc>an infinite matrix. The first entry of this equation is the Riccati equation of the standard linearization at the equilibrium.The lifted equation has a structure of its own that characterizes the exact solution, and this paper exploits it.

The series comes from the Hamilton-Jacobi–Bellman (HJB) equation. Optimal control seeks a control law that minimizes a given cost functional [4]. Dynamic programming [5] reduces this problem to the HJB equation, a nonlinear partial differential equation whose solution is the value function [6]. For nonlinear systems, the equation rarely has a closed-form solution, and a smooth solution may not exist globally [7]. One therefore turns to approximations, such as Galerkin projection [8] and polynomial approximation [9]. The power series method of Al’brekht and Lukes is one of them. It computes the Maclaurin coefficients of the value function one degree at a time. It has been applied to bilinear systems [10] and to systems with additive control [11]. The method is local by nature. Adding terms improves the accuracy near the equilibrium, but it does not enlarge the region where the series is valid [3].

Carleman linearization lifts a nonlinear finite-dimensional system to an infinite-dimensional bilinear one [12]-[14]. It is the dynamical systems analogue of the Maclaurin expansion, as the state is replaced by the sequence of its monomials, and the nonlinear vector field by an infinite state matrix. The idea extends to Fourier bases [15], [16]. It also underlies quantum algorithms for nonlinear differential equations [17], [18]. Related lifts to higher-dimensional linear models have been used to compute invariant sets [19]. Carleman linearization has also been used to extend the Lyapunov equation to nonlinear systems [20] and to estimate domains of attraction [21]. In both cases, the lifted equation is linear in the unknown. The price of the lift is that the resulting operators are unbounded. In practice, they must be truncated [14], [22].

In earlier work, we lifted the HJB equation itself [23], [24]. This produced an infinite-dimensional equation, quadratic and symmetric in the unknown, that resembles an algebraic Riccati equation. We also gave an iterative algorithm to solve it. However, one term of that equation contained an operator that depends on the unknown only implicitly. This operator concealed the structure of the equation. Since then, truncations of the lifted equation have been learned from data [25], [26]. A related Riccati-like operator equation has also been derived in a Koopman framework [27]. None of these works gives the solution of the lifted equation in explicit form. Without it, one cannot check what the equation actually computes. This is where the scalar case helps. For a scalar system, the HJB equation is quadratic in the derivative of the value function and has a closed-form solution. Every claim about<tbc>

the lifted equation can therefore be checked exactly, as was done for scalar bilinear systems in \[10\]. We focus on the scalar case, where the structure of the lifted equation can be shown explicitly, as a first step towards multivariable systems.

For scalar systems, our contributions are threefold. First, we eliminate the implicit operator. The lifted HJB equation then becomes a Riccati-type equation for a lower-triangular Toeplitz matrix. Second, we show that, under controllability of the linearization and detectability of the cost, this equation has a unique solution with positive diagonal entries. The solution is obtained from the scalar Riccati equation of the linearized problem, followed by a sequence of scalar linear equations. It is a bounded operator whenever the Maclaurin coefficients of the derivative of the value function decay fast enough. Third, we prove that the finite sections of this solution converge exponentially to the derivative of the value function near the origin. Numerical simulations illustrate the results, and Fig. 1 summarizes the approach and the role of the theorems.

## II. PROBLEM STATEMENT

We start from Al’brekht’s 1961 problem \[1\] and specialize it to one state and one input, which is its simplest nonlinear case. Its solution has a closed form, which serves as a benchmark as it tells us what the lifted HJB equation must compute. In this section, we state the problem, list our assumptions, and give the solution.

The system is input-affine,

\(\dot{x}=f(x)+g(x)u,x(0)=x_0\in\mathbb{R},\) (1)

with input \(u\in\mathbb{R}\). We assume that _f_(0)=0 and that _f_ and _g_ are analytic around the origin, with Maclaurin expansions

\(f(x)=\sum_{k=1}^\infty f_kx^k\text{and}g(x)=\sum_{k=0}^\infty g_kx^k.\) (2)

The cost to be minimized is

\(J(x_0,u)=\int_0^\infty\big(q(x(t))+ru^2(t)\big)dt,\) (3)

where _r\>_0 weights the control and the state cost _q_ satisfies the following condition.

**Detectability.** The state cost \(q:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_+\) is nonnegative, and _f_ and _q_ have no common zero other than the origin, i.e., \(q(x)\ge 0\) for all _x_ and _f(x_)=_q(x_)=0 only if _x_=0. In addition, _q_ is analytic around the origin with

\(q(x)=\sum_{k=2}^\infty q_kx^k\text{with}q_2>0.\) (4)

The second part of (4), along with the condition that _f_ and _q_ have no common zero other than the origin, says that the origin is the only rest point of zero cost. This is zero-state detectability of (_f,q_) \[28\]. The condition _q_<sub>2</sub>_\>_0 means that the linearized pair \((\sqrt{q_2},f_1)\) is observable.

Let _V(x_<sub>0</sub>)=inf_<sub>u</sub>J(x_<sub>0</sub>_,u_) be the value function, and let _V<sub>x</sub>_ denote its derivative. Dynamic programming gives

\(min_{u\in\mathbb{R}}\big\{V_x\big(f(x)+g(x)u\big)+q(x)+ru^2\big\}=0.\) (5)

The expression in braces is a convex quadratic in _u_. Its minimizer is the optimal feedback

\(u^*(x)=-\frac{1}{2r}g(x)V_x.\) (6)

Substituting (6) into (5) gives the HJB equation

\(V_xf(x)-\frac{1}{4r}(V_xg(x))^2+q(x)=0.\) (7)

The optimal feedback is known as soon as _V<sub>x</sub>_ is. The rest of the paper is about _V<sub>x</sub>_.

**Controllability.** The linearization of (1) at the origin is \(\dot{x}=f_1x+g_0u\). We assume that it is controllable,

\(g_0\neq 0.\) (8)

**Existence.** Let us define

\(\Delta:=f_1^2+\frac{1}{r}q_2g_0^2.\) (9)

By (4) and (8), \(\Delta>0\). The numbers \(\pm\sqrt{\Delta}\) are the eigenvalues of the Hamiltonian matrix of the linearized problem. The coefficient of _x_<sup>2</sup> in (7) is its Riccati equation,

\(q_2+f_1v-\frac{g_0^2}{4r}v^2=0,v=V_{xx}(0).\) (10)

Its roots are \(v=2rg_0^{-2}(f_1\pm\sqrt{\Delta})\). They are real and have opposite signs, because _q_<sub>2</sub>_\>_0. The positive root, \(v=2rg_0^{-2}(f_1+\sqrt{\Delta})\), gives the closed-loop pole \(f_1-\frac{g_0^2}{2r}v=-\sqrt{\Delta}\). As done by Al’brekht, the recursion shown in this paper starts from the mentioned root.

**Closed-form solution.** The recursion is not needed to find _V<sub>x</sub>_. The HJB equation (7) is quadratic in the single unknown _V<sub>x</sub>_, and it can be solved in closed form. Let

\(l(x):=x^{-2}f(x)^2+r^{-1}x^{-2}q(x)g(x)^2.\) (11)

By (2) and (4), _l_ is analytic around the origin with \(l(0)=\Delta>0\). By (4), _l(x)\>_0 for \(x\neq 0\) wherever \(g(x)\neq 0\). Among the solutions of (7) that are twice differentiable at the origin, exactly one has _V<sub>xx</sub>_(0)_\>_0:

\(V_x=\frac{2r\big(f(x)+x\sqrt{l(x)}\big)}{g(x)^2}.\) (12)

The other one has \(V_{xx}(0)=2rg_0^{-2}(f_1-\sqrt{\Delta})<0\). To see this, note that for \(x\neq 0\) a solution must coincide with one of the two branches \(2r\big(f\pm\sqrt{f^2+qg^2/r}\big)/g^2\), which are distinct because _l\>_0. If _V<sub>xx</sub>_(0) exists, the one-sided slopes at the origin must agree, and this leaves the two analytic functions \(2r(f\pm x\sqrt{l})/g^2\). By (6), the optimal feedback is

\(u^*(x)=-\frac{f(x)+x\sqrt{l(x)}}{g(x)}\)

and the optimal closed-loop system is

\(\dot{x}=f(x)+g(x)u^*(x)=-x\sqrt{l(x)}.\) (13)

On any interval around the origin where \(g\neq 0\), the closed loop in (13) strictly decreases |_x_|. The origin is

therefore asymptotically stable under _u_<sup>∗</sup>, with linearization \(\dot{x}=-\sqrt{\Delta}x\). The function \(V(x)=\int_0^xV_x(s)ds\) is positive definite. Since _f_, _g_ and _l_ are analytic around the origin with \(g(0)=g_0\neq 0\) and \(l(0)=\Delta>0\), the function _V<sub>x</sub>_ in (12) is analytic around the origin:

\(V_x=\sum_{k=1}^\infty v_kx^k,x\in(-\rho,\rho).\) (14)

Here \(\rho\) is any number below the radius of convergence. By Cauchy’s estimate, there is a constant \(M=M(\rho)\) such that

\(|v_k|\le M\rho^{-k},k\ge 1.\) (15)

The radius of convergence is set by the complex singularities of _V<sub>x</sub>_, such as the complex zeros of _g_ and of _l_. It can be smaller than the real interval on which (12) is defined. We return to this point in Section IV.

While the closed form solves the scalar problem, it does not show how the coefficients _v<sub>k</sub>_ fit together. In the next section, we lift the HJB equation by Carleman linearization. We then show that all of the coefficients _v<sub>k</sub>_ solve a single infinite-dimensional Riccati-type equation whose first entry is the Riccati equation (10).

## III. HJB EQUATION FOR CARLEMAN LINEARIZATION

Carleman linearization replaces the scalar state _x_ by the sequence of its powers \[12\], \[13\]. In the new variables, the nonlinear system (1) becomes an infinite-dimensional bilinear system. We first write this system down and then lift the HJB equation along with it. The Carleman lifting operator is the infinite-dimensional nonlinear map

\(\Psi(x):=\text{col}[x,x^2,x^3,\dots],\) (16)

where col\[_v,w_\] stacks the column vector _v_ on top of the vector _w_. Along a trajectory of (1), each power satisfies \(\frac{d}{dt}x^m=mx^{m-1}\big(f(x)+g(x)u\big)\). Expanding _x_<sup>_m_-1</sup>_f(x_) and _x_<sup>_m_-1</sup>_g(x_) by (2) gives the Carleman linearization

\(\dot{\Psi}=\mathbf{D}\big(\mathbf{A}\Psi+(\mathbf{B}\Psi+\mathbf{b}_0)u\big),\) (17)

where the operators are defined by

\(\mathbf{A}=\left[\begin{array}{ c c c c c }
f_1 & f_2 & f_3 & \cdots &  \\
0 & f_1 & f_2 & \cdots &  \\
0 & 0 & f_1 & \cdots &  \\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots &  \\
\end{array}\right],\mathbf{B}=\left[\begin{array}{ c c c c c c }
g_1 & g_2 & g_3 & \cdots &  \\
g_0 & g_1 & g_2 & \cdots &  \\
0 & g_0 & g_1 & \cdots &  \\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots &  \\
\end{array}\right]\) (18)

\(\mathbf{D}=\left[\begin{array}{ c c c c c }
1 & 0 & 0 & \cdots &  \\
0 & 2 & 0 & \cdots &  \\
0 & 0 & 3 & \cdots &  \\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots &  \\
\end{array}\right],\mathbf{b}_0=g_0\mathbf{e}_1=\left[\begin{array}{ c }
g_0 \\
0 \\
0 \\
\vdots
\end{array}\right]\) (19)

and \(\mathbf{e}_1=[1,0,0,\dots]^\unknown\). The structure of these matrices is the point of this section. **A** is upper-triangular Toeplitz, with the Maclaurin coefficients of _f_ along its rows. **B** is upper Hessenberg Toeplitz, with the coefficients of _g_ along its rows<tbc>

<tbc>and _g_<sub>0</sub> on the subdiagonal. On the lifted state they act as multiplication operators:

\(\mathbf{A}\Psi=x^{-1}f(x)\Psi,\mathbf{B}\Psi+\mathbf{b}_0=x^{-1}g(x)\Psi,\) (20)

because the _m_-th entries of the two sides are _x_<sup>_m_-1</sup>_f(x_) and _x_<sup>_m_-1</sup>_g(x_). These two identities are all we need from the lift. In this section, we study the HJB equation of (17), and in Section IV we prove exponential convergence of its finite-section approximations; see Figure 1.

The cost lifts in the same way. By (4),

\(q(x)=\Psi^\top\mathbf{Q}\Psi,\) (21)

where \(\mathbf{Q}=[q(i,j)]_{i,j=1}^\infty\) is the symmetric tridiagonal matrix with _q(i,i_)=_q_<sub>2_i_</sub>_,q(i,i_+1)=_q(i_+1_,i_)=_q_<sub>2_i_+1</sub>/2 for \(i\ge 1\), and _q(i,j_)=0 otherwise. Following the quadratization procedure in \[24\], we view the value function as a function of \(\Psi\) and write \(V_\Psi\) for its gradient. The HJB equation for the lifted system (17) is then

\(V_\Psi^\top\mathbf{DA}\Psi-\frac{1}{4r}\big(V_\Psi^\top\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{B}\Psi+\mathbf{b}_0)\big)^2+\Psi^\top\mathbf{Q}\Psi=0,\) (22)

and the corresponding optimal control law is

\(u^*=-\frac{1}{2r}(\mathbf{B}\Psi+\mathbf{b}_0)^\top\mathbf{D}V_\Psi.\) (23)

By the chain rule, \(V_x=V_\Psi^\top\frac{d\Psi}{dx}=x^{-1}V_\Psi^\top\mathbf{D}\Psi\). Together with (20), this shows that on the lifted state (22) and (23) are the HJB equation (7) and the feedback (6) of Section II. Lifting therefore leaves the HJB equation unchanged on the lifted state and expresses it through the lifted operators, whose structure is exploited next.

We look for a solution whose gradient is linear in \(\Psi\),

\(\mathbf{D}V_\Psi=2\mathbf{P}\Psi\) (24)

for some infinite matrix \(\mathbf{P}=[p(i,j)]_{i,j=1}^\infty\). Then, \(V_x=2x^{-1}\Psi^\top\mathbf{P}\Psi\). Since \(\Psi^\top\mathbf{P}\Psi=\sum_{i,j=1}^\infty p(i,j)x^{i+j}\), the matrix **P** enters only through the sums of its anti-diagonal entries,

\(\pi_m(\mathbf{P})=\pi_m(\mathbf{P}^\top)=\sum_{i=1}^{m-1}p(i,m-i)\) (25)

for all \(m\ge 2\) and \(V_x=2\sum_{m=2}^\infty\pi_m(\mathbf{P})x^{m-1}\). Comparing with (14), the Maclaurin coefficients of _Vx_ are \(v_{m-1}=2\pi_m(\mathbf{P})\). We collect the anti-diagonal sums in the lower- triangular Toeplitz matrix \(\unknown:=\left[\begin{array}{ c c c c } \pi_2(\mathbf{P}) & 0 & 0 & \cdots \\ \pi_3(\mathbf{P}) & \pi_2(\mathbf{P}) & 0 & \cdots \\ \pi_4(\mathbf{P}) & \pi_3(\mathbf{P}) & \pi_2(\mathbf{P}) & \cdots \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots \end{array}\right].\) (26) Many matrices **P** have the same anti-diagonal sums. They all give the same _Vx_, and \(\unknown\) is what they have in common. The next theorem rewrites the HJB equation (22) and the control law (23) in terms of \(\unknown\) alone. Let us denote \(\mathbf{f}=[f_1,f_2,f_3,\dots]^\top\), \(\mathbf{g}=[g_0,g_1,g_2,\dots]^\top\), and \(\bar{\mathbf{A}}=\mathbf{f}\mathbf{e}_1^\top\). _Theorem 1:_ Suppose that **A**, **B**, **P**, **Q**, and \(\unknown\) are as in (18), (19), (24), (21), and (26). Under the ansatz (24), the lifted HJB equation (22) is equivalent to \(\Psi^\top\left(\unknown\bar{\mathbf{A}}+\bar{\mathbf{A}}^\top\unknown^\top+\mathbf{Q}-\frac{1}{r}\unknown\mathbf{g}\mathbf{g}^\top\unknown^\top\right)\Psi=0,\) (27) and the control law (23) becomes \(u^*=-\frac{1}{r}\Psi^\top\unknown\mathbf{g}.\) (28) The proof is given in Appendix A. Before we use the theorem, we point out what it implies. Equation (27) has the form of an algebraic Riccati equation, \(PA+A^\top P+Q-\frac{1}{r}Pbb^\top P=0\), with \(\unknown\) in the role of _P_. The data are read off the lift where **f** is the first row of **A**, **g** is the second row of **B**, and **Q** is the lifted cost. The unknown is a single sequence, \(\pi_2,\pi_3,\dots\), which, for the solution of Theorem 2, is the sequence of Maclaurin coefficients of _Vx_ up to the factor two. In our earlier work \[24\], the quadratic term of the lifted equation contained an auxiliary operator that depended on the unknown only implicitly. Here that operator is gone. The quadratic term is \(\unknown\mathbf{g}\mathbf{g}^\top\unknown^\top\), explicit and of rank one, as in the single-input linear-quadratic case; along \(\Psi(x)\) it gives \(\frac{1}{r}(\Psi^\top\unknown\mathbf{g})^2=r\left(u^*\right)^2\), the control cost. The (1,1) entry of the matrix in (27) is \(2f_1\pi_2+q_2-\frac{g_0^2}{r}\pi_2^2\). With \(v=2\pi_2\), this is the Riccati equation (10) of the linearization. The infinite Riccati equation thus contains the finite one as its first entry, and the rest of its entries hold the nonlinear terms. Two facts explain why the lift produces an equation with a Riccati form rather than something more complicated. First, by (20), the Carleman vector \(\Psi(x)\) is an eigenvector of **A** with eigenvalue _f(x)/x_, and the analogous relation holds for **B**. Thus, the lifted equation depends on **P** only through the series \(\sum_{m=2}^\infty\pi_m(\mathbf{P})x^m\). Second, products of power series are represented by products of lower-triangular Toeplitz matrices. The matrix \(\unknown\) is the Toeplitz matrix of the series \(\sum_{m=2}^\infty\pi_m(\mathbf{P})x^{m-2}\), and for any sequence \(\mathbf{c}=[c_0,c_1,\dots]^\top\) with generating function _c(x_), \(\Psi^\top\unknown\mathbf{c}=x\left(\sum_{m=2}^\infty\pi_m(\mathbf{P})x^{m-2}\right)c(x).\) (29) This identity turns every product in the HJB equation into a matrix product; both identities in the proof of Theorem 1 are instances of it. We should highlight that (27) is an identity between quadratic forms evaluated along the curve \(\Psi(x)\). It says that every anti-diagonal sum of the matrix in parentheses vanishes, which is one scalar equation per degree. It does not say that the matrix vanishes entry by entry. Theorem 1 writes the lifted HJB equation in terms of \(\unknown\) alone, but (27) is still infinite-dimensional. The next corollary closes the loop with Section II. The first column of \(\unknown\) defines a function that solves the scalar HJB equation (7), and the lifted feedback (28) is the feedback (6). This is what allows us to compute \(\unknown\) degree by degree in Section IV and to compare its finite sections with _Vx_ in (12). _Corollary 1:_ Let \(\unknown\) be a lower-triangular Toeplitz matrix of the form (26) that satisfies (27), and set \(U(x):=2\Psi^\top\unknown\mathbf{e}_1=2\sum_{m=2}^\infty\pi_m(\mathbf{P})x^{m-1}.\) (30) Then, \(U(x)=2x^{-1}\Psi^\top\mathbf{P}\Psi\) and the function _U_ satisfies the HJB equation \(q(x)+U(x)f(x)-\frac{1}{4r}\big(g(x)U(x)\big)^2=0,\) (31) and the control (28) equals \(u^*=-\frac{1}{2r}g(x)U(x)\), as in (6). Conversely, let _U_ be analytic around the origin with _U_(0)=0 and satisfy (31). Then, the Toeplitz matrix \(\unknown\) whose entries \(\pi_m\) are one half of the coefficient of _x__m_-1 in _U_ satisfies (27). The proof is given in Appendix B. In words, the lifted Riccati-type equation and the scalar HJB equation have the same solutions. _Remark 1:_ By (24) and the chain rule, \(V_x=\frac{dV}{d\Psi}\frac{d\Psi}{dx}=x^{-1}V_\Psi^\top\mathbf{D}\Psi=2x^{-1}\Psi^\top\mathbf{P}\Psi=U(x).\) (32) Thus, the function _U_ in (30) is the derivative of the lifted value function along \(\Psi(x)\). Along the closed loop, (31) and (28) give \(\dot{V}=V_x\big(f(x)+g(x)u^*\big)=-\Psi^\top\mathbf{Q}\Psi-\frac{1}{r}\Psi^\top\unknown\mathbf{g}\mathbf{g}^\top\unknown^\top\Psi\)
\(=-q(x)-r\left|u^*(x)\right|^2\le 0.\) This is the Lyapunov inequality one expects from an HJB equation. Moreover, the solution constructed in Theorem 2 has \(\pi_2(\mathbf{P})>0\) by (33), and _U_ is analytic with \(U'(0)=2\pi_2(\mathbf{P})>0\). By Section II, there is only one such solution of the HJB equation. Hence, _U_ is the closed-form _Vx_ in (12), the closed-loop system is \(\dot{x}=-x\sqrt{l(x)}\) as in (13), the origin is asymptotically stable in the sense of Lyapunov, and _V_ is the value function of the problem. Thus, the positive-diagonal solution of the lifted Riccati-type equation gives the optimal cost while serving as a Lyapunov function. ## IV. EXPONENTIAL CONVERGENCE OF FINITE-SECTION APPROXIMATIONS By Theorem 1, solving the lifted HJB equation (22) amounts to finding the lower-triangular Toeplitz solution \(\unknown\)

of the Riccati-type equation (27). In this section, we solve this equation by a recursion of scalar equations, and we show that the finite-sections of the solution converge exponentially to _Vx_ near the origin. _Theorem 2:_ Suppose that the system (1) with _f_, _g_ and _q_ satisfying (2), (4) and (8), and let \(\Delta>0\) be as in (9). Then, the Riccati-type equation (27) has exactly one lower- triangular Toeplitz solution \(\unknown\) with positive diagonal entries, where its diagonal entry is \(\pi_2(\mathbf{P})=rg_0^{-2}(f_1+\sqrt{\Delta}),\) (33) and its remaining entries \(\pi_{m+2}(\mathbf{P})\), for \(m\ge 1\), are given recursively by \(\pi_{m+2}(\mathbf{P})=(2\sqrt{\Delta})^{-1}\big(q_{m+2}\)
\(+2\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\big(f_{m-k+1}-g_0g_{m-k}\pi_2(\mathbf{P})/r\big)\pi_{k+2}(\mathbf{P})\)
\(-\frac{1}{r}\sum_{n=1}^{m-1}\sum_{j=0}^n\sum_{j^\prime=0}^{m-n}g_{n-j}g_{m-n-j^\prime}\pi_{j+2}(\mathbf{P})\pi_{j^\prime+2}(\mathbf{P})\big).\) (34) Moreover, \(2\pi_m(\mathbf{P})=v_{m-1}\) for all \(m\ge 2\), where _vk_ are the Maclaurin coefficients of _Vx_ in (14). The proof is given in Appendix C. The recursion deserves a closer look. Its first equation, the case _m_=0, is the Riccati equation (10) of the linearization, and (33) is its positive solution. Every later equation is linear in the new unknown \(\pi_{m+2}(\mathbf{P})\), and the coefficient in front of it is always the same number, \(-2\sqrt{\Delta}\), which is twice the closed-loop pole of Section II. The right-hand side involves only the data _fk_, _gk_, _qk_ and the entries already computed. This is Al’breht’s recursion for the scalar case, with one difference: _here it is read off a single matrix equation, degree by degree, rather than derived anew at each degree_. Two consequences follow. Existence and uniqueness of the solution are decided entirely by the first equation, since \(\Delta>0\) makes every later pivot nonzero. And, the first _N_ equations involve only \(\pi_2(\mathbf{P}),\dots,\pi_{N+1}(\mathbf{P})\). Therefore, truncating the equation and truncating the solution give the same result. The finite-section of the solution is the exact solution of the finite-section. No truncation error is introduced by the recursion. Let us consider the finite-section of order \(N\ge 1\), \(\unknown_N=\left[\begin{array}{ c c c c c c } \pi_2(\mathbf{P}) & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\ \pi_3(\mathbf{P}) & \pi_2(\mathbf{P}) & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\ \pi_4(\mathbf{P}) & \pi_3(\mathbf{P}) & \pi_2(\mathbf{P}) & \cdots & 0 \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \ddots \\ \pi_{N+1}(\mathbf{P}) & \pi_N(\mathbf{P}) & \pi_{N-1}(\mathbf{P}) & \cdots & \pi_2(\mathbf{P}) \end{array}\right],\) (35) of the matrix \(\unknown\) in (26), and define \(U_N(x)=2\Psi_N^\top\unknown_N\mathbf{e}_1,\) (36) where \(\Psi_N=[x,x^2,\dots,x^N]^\top\). By Theorem 2, \(U_N(x)=\sum_{k=1}^Nv_kx^k\) is the Taylor polynomial of degree _N_ of _Vx_. The next theorem gives the rate at which _UN_ converges to _Vx_. _Theorem 3:_ Suppose that the system (1) with _f_, _g_ and _q_ satisfying (2), (4) and (8), and let _Vx_ be the solution (12) of the HJB equation (7). Let \(\pi_m(\mathbf{P})\), for \(m\ge 2\), be as in (33) and (34), and let \(\unknown_N\) and _UN_ be as in (35) and (36). Then, \(|U_N(x)-V_x|\le M(1-|x|/\rho)^{-1}|x/\rho|^N\) (37) for all \(x\in(-\rho,\rho)\) and \(N\ge 1\), where _M_ and \(\rho\) are the constants in (15). The proof is given in Appendix D. The bound is exponential in _N_ with ratio \(|x|/\rho\). Each additional row of \(\unknown_N\) reduces the error by this factor. The constant \(\rho\) is any number below the radius of convergence of _Vx_, and, as noted in Section II, that radius is set by the complex singularities of _Vx_. It can be smaller than the real interval on which (12) is defined, in which case the finite-sections converge only on \((-\rho,\rho)\) even though _Vx_ is defined beyond it. The truncated feedback \(u_N^*(x):=-\frac{1}{r}g(x)U_N(x)\) inherits the bound with an extra factor |_g(x_)|/(2_r_). The state matrix **DA** arising in the Carleman linearization (17) is unbounded, whereas the Riccati-type solution \(\unknown\) of the corresponding HJB equation need not be. In fact, as shown in the following remark, \(\unknown\) is a bounded operator whenever the Maclaurin coefficients of _Vx_ exhibit sufficiently fast decay. This distinction highlights that the unboundedness of the lifted dynamics does not preclude the existence of a well-behaved solution to the associated HJB equation. _Remark 2:_ For an infinite matrix \(\mathbf{C}=[c(i,j)]_{i,j=1}^\infty\), define its Schur norm by \(\|\mathbf{C}\|_\mathcal{S}=max\left\{sup_{i\ge 1}\sum_{j=1}^\infty|c(i,j)|,sup_{j\ge 1}\sum_{i=1}^\infty|c(i,j)|\right\}.\) Suppose that the radius of convergence of _Vx_ in (14) exceeds one, and choose \(\rho>1\) in (15). Since \(\unknown\) is lower-triangular Toeplitz, every column sum equals \(\sum_{m=2}^\infty|\pi_m(\mathbf{P})|\), and by \(2\pi_m(\mathbf{P})=v_{m-1}\) and (15), \(\|\unknown\|_\mathcal{S}=\sum_{m=2}^\infty|\pi_m(\mathbf{P})|\le\frac{M}{2}\sum_{m=2}^\infty\rho^{-(m-1)}=\frac{M}{2(\rho-1)}.\) By the Schur test, \(\unknown\) is then a bounded operator on \(\ell^p\) for every \(1\le p\le\infty\), where \(\ell^p\) is the Banach space of _p_- summable sequences \(\{c(k)\}_{k=1}^\infty\) with its standard norm. The threshold one reflects the choice of unit weights. On the weighted space with norm \(\|c\|_{p,\sigma}:=\big(\sum_{k=1}^\infty|c(k)|^p\sigma^{kp}\big)^{1/p}\) for \(1\le p<\infty\) and \(\|c\|_{\infty,\sigma}=sup_{k\ge 1}|c(k)|\sigma^k\), the same computation shows that \(\unknown\) is bounded for every \(0<\sigma<\rho\). ## V. CONCLUSION Al’brekht’s method solves one Riccati equation and then an endless sequence of linear equations. We asked what these equations add up to. For scalar analytic input-affine systems, Carleman linearization gave the answer. They are the entries of a single infinite-dimensional Riccati equation in a lower- triangular Toeplitz matrix. The familiar Riccati equation of the standard linearization at the equilibrium is its first entry. The nonlinear terms fill the entries below it. The lifted equation has exactly one solution with positive diagonal entries. That solution is the derivative of the value function, and its finite sections converge to it exponentially. What is new is not the solution. In the scalar case, it has a closed form, and that closed form served as our benchmark. What is new is the structure the lift reveals: a Riccati equation that is decided by its first entry and solved exactly, one entry at a time. After lifting, the equation of linear optimal control and the equation of nonlinear optimal control are the same equation. Nothing in this structure depends on the state dimension. The extension to general nonlinear systems is the natural next step. ## APPENDIX ### A.
